title: The Black Death

cards.h: The worst disaster in European history began with a sick ship
cards.b:
In October 1347, a few Genoese ships docked at Messina in Sicily. Many sailors were dead. Those alive were covered with black swellings that oozed.

The port authorities ordered them out. Too late. The Black Death had arrived.

The disease is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, confirmed by DNA from plague-pit skeletons. It was usually spread by fleas on rats, though it could also spread from person to person in its lung form.

Historians estimate that about a third to a half of Europeans died in 1347-1351. Estimates differ, and some areas were barely touched. Cities with crowded streets suffered most. In the Middle East and North Africa, too, millions died.

Victims got fever, black swellings called buboes, and many died within days. Doctors had no cure. Many blamed bad air or the stars.

Some people whipped themselves in public, the Flagellants, hoping to please God. Others blamed Jews and attacked communities, for example in Strasbourg in 1349. The Pope condemned the violence, but it went on.

By 1377 the port of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) required ships to wait for 30 days; Venice later made it 40 (quaranta giorni), which gives us 'quarantine'.

So many workers died that survivors could demand higher wages. In England, laws tried to freeze wages, which angered people. The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 followed, partly from this anger.

Some historians say that, in the long run, the Black Death weakened serfdom in Western Europe.

Plague came back in waves for 400 years: London's Great Plague in 1665 and Marseille in 1720. Europe slowly learned about quarantine and isolation.

The plague was not a one-time event but a recurring shadow.

cards.h: Is 'Ring a Ring o' Roses' about the plague?
cards.b:
Myth: the nursery rhyme describes plague symptoms.Fact: there is no evidence for that. The rhyme was first written down in the late 1800s. Folklorists say the plague link was added in the 20th century.

Another point: rats were not alone. Some researchers argue that human fleas and lice also helped spread it. That is still being tested.

Bombay 1896

The Black Death's cousin came to India in September 1896, when plague arrived in Bombay by sea from Hong Kong. This was the third plague pandemic, and India would lose more than 12 million people by the 1920s.

Waldemar Haffkine made a vaccine at Bombay's Plague Research Laboratory in 1897. Harsh British measures, such as house searches, caused anger. In 1897 W. C. Rand was shot at Pune by the Chapekar brothers.

The Epidemic Diseases Act of 1897, passed in that crisis, was still in force when Covid-19 struck in 2020.

Five things to remember

  1. The Black Death hit Europe in 1347-1351.
  2. Yersinia pestis is the confirmed cause.
  3. Perhaps a third to a half of Europeans died.
  4. Quarantine began in Ragusa and Venice.
  5. India's plague came in 1896.

Think about it

  • How do societies change after a huge loss of workers?
  • Why do people look for scapegoats in a panic?
